subject: psychology
title: Forensic Psychology: Explanations of Offending
welcome_lead: Genes, brains, personality, learning, society — many roads to crime.
meta_desc: A-Level Psychology explanations of offending: genetic, neural, Eysenck's personality theory.
final_note: Crime is biopsychosocial — never one cause.

concepts.def: Region for impulse control — often less active in offenders.
Sutherland — crime learned from those around us.

walkthroughs.body_html: Brunner et al. (1993) studied a Dutch family with abnormally low MAOA enzyme levels and high rates of violence. Raine et al. (1997) PET-scanned 41 murderers — reduced activity in the prefrontal cortex and asymmetry in the amygdala. Genes don't determine, but they tilt the odds.

Eysenck (1964) argued criminals score high on Psychoticism, Extraversion and Neuroticism. Extraverts need stimulation; neurotics are unstable; high-P types are aggressive. Farrington et al. (1982) partly supported the link, especially for P, but found E and N inconsistent.

Kohlberg (1958): offenders are stuck at the pre-conventional level of moral reasoning. Cognitive distortions include hostile attribution bias (ambiguous behaviour seen as threat) and minimalisation (denying severity). CBT challenges distortions.
